questions.passage:
• The Elm Street community garden opened in 2018 with 18 raised beds.
• In 2024, 45 volunteer gardeners grew 1,200 pounds of vegetables.
• The garden donates half of its produce to a pantry two blocks away.
• The city has approved an unused lot for a second garden, but the garden group needs volunteers and tools.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a flyer recruiting volunteers that emphasizes the garden’s community impact. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Elm Street community garden opened in 2018 with 18 raised beds and now has a second site available.
In 2024, volunteer gardeners at the Elm Street community garden grew 1,200 pounds of vegetables and donated half to a nearby pantry.
The garden is two blocks from a pantry and uses raised beds.
The city has approved an unused lot for a second garden, so the group needs volunteers and tools.
questions.explanation: The sentence combining the 2024 harvest total with the donation to a nearby pantry shows the garden’s concrete community impact while also mentioning volunteer gardeners, which suits a recruitment flyer. The note about the approved lot stresses a need for volunteers and tools but does not show impact, and the opening date and bed count are background details rather than evidence of impact.

questions.passage: The first trial produced no measurable change in the material’s strength ______ the researchers decided to repeat the experiment with a larger sample.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: therefore,
; and therefore,
, therefore,
; therefore,
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by the conjunctive adverb 'therefore,' so a semicolon must precede it and a comma must follow it. A comma before 'therefore' creates a comma splice, and omitting the semicolon leaves the clauses fused. The semicolon-plus-'and' construction is not the standard way to join these clauses.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Each of the volunteers who ______ at the food pantry on Saturday mornings receives a brief training session before the doors open.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: is working
work
has worked
works
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural noun 'volunteers,' so the verb in the relative clause must be plural: 'work.' The main verb 'receives' is singular because its subject is 'Each,' but that does not make the verb inside the 'who' clause singular.

questions.passage: For years, a team of archaeologists assumed that the stone walls on a windswept island were the remains of a single fortress. New surveys, however, show that the walls were built in at least three separate phases over two centuries. The earliest sections were low boundaries around small farm plots; later residents raised them and added watchtowers. Rather than a sudden military project, the walls record a long, gradual response to changing land use and a growing need to defend stored grain.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The walls were built suddenly by a military force.
The island’s stone walls were built and modified over a long period for changing purposes, not as one fortress.
Watchtowers were the earliest stone structures on the island.
Archaeologists have learned that the island’s residents abandoned farming.
questions.explanation: The text explains that the walls were built in several phases over two centuries, first as farm boundaries and later with watchtowers, so they reflect changing land use and defense needs rather than one fortress. The statement about a sudden military project contradicts the passage, and the other choices misstate the earliest structures or invent an abandonment of farming.

questions.passage: The first survey identified only two nests in the meadow______ the second survey, conducted at night, found more than forty.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: , and but
but
, but
; but
questions.explanation: The sentence joins two independent clauses that contrast: the first survey found few nests, but the second found many. A comma before the coordinating conjunction 'but' correctly marks the boundary. A semicolon before 'but' is not standard here, and omitting the comma or adding 'and but' creates an ungrammatical clause boundary.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The bridge repair on Route 9 is now delayed until next spring. Had the city council approved the funding measure earlier, construction ______ before the rainy season.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: would have begun
will have begun
would begin
had begun
questions.explanation: This sentence describes a past unreal condition: the council did not approve the measure earlier, and the expected result would have occurred before the rainy season. The correct construction is 'Had ... approved ..., construction would have begun.' 'Would begin' uses the wrong conditional form, and 'will have begun' wrongly shifts to the future.

questions.passage: For decades, city planners treated vacant lots as temporary gaps in the urban landscape. Recent work by a team of ecologists suggests that these lots can become small but valuable habitats. In a survey of 60 vacant parcels, the team found that lots mowed only twice a year supported nearly twice as many bee species as lots mowed monthly. The researchers caution that not every vacant lot should be left alone: sites near busy roads still need regular maintenance to control invasive plants and trash. Still, they argue, simple changes in mowing schedules could turn many unused spaces into pollinator refuges at little cost.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Vacant lots should always be left unmowed to protect bees.
Lots near busy roads support more bee species than lots mowed monthly.
City planners have stopped treating vacant lots as temporary gaps.
With modest changes in maintenance, many vacant urban lots could provide valuable habitat for pollinators.
questions.explanation: The passage’s main point is that vacant lots, with relatively low-cost changes such as less frequent mowing, can become valuable pollinator habitat. The absolute claim that every lot should be left unmowed conflicts with the caution about busy roads, and the other choices overstate the evidence or reverse a detail.

questions.passage:
• Riverside Community Kitchen serves free lunches five days a week.
• In 2023, it served 38,000 meals, up from 27,000 in 2022.
• Demand is highest on Mondays, when the kitchen often runs out of food by 12:30 p.m.
• The kitchen’s current storage space is too small to accept large donations of fresh produce.
• A local grocery chain has offered to donate surplus vegetables if the kitchen can add refrigeration.
questions.q: The student wants to write a sentence for a fundraising letter that emphasizes both growing demand and the need for a specific upgrade. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The kitchen’s current storage space is too small, and a local grocery chain has offered to donate surplus vegetables.
As demand rose from 27,000 meals in 2022 to 38,000 in 2023, with Monday lunches often running out by 12:30 p.m., the kitchen needs added refrigeration to accept donated fresh produce.
In 2023, the kitchen served 38,000 meals, up from 27,000 in 2022.
The Riverside Community Kitchen serves free lunches five days a week and receives surplus vegetables from a local grocery chain.
questions.explanation: The fundraising sentence needs to show demand has grown and identify the upgrade that would allow the kitchen to accept produce. The sentence citing the meal increase and Monday shortages while requesting refrigeration for donated vegetables accomplishes both goals. The notes about serving lunch or storage alone do not combine growth in demand with the refrigeration upgrade.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The photographer’s early portraits hang in the first gallery, while the later works fill three more rooms and a small theater. Walking through the new exhibit at the city museum, ______.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the photographer’s early portraits seemed startlingly modern to many visitors
many visitors were startled by the modernity of the photographer’s early portraits
the early portraits by the photographer were startlingly modern to many visitors
the modernity of the photographer’s early portraits startled many visitors
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase 'Walking through the new exhibit' must modify the subject of the main clause: the people who are walking, not the portraits or their modernity. 'Many visitors were startled...' supplies that subject. The choices beginning with 'the photographer’s early portraits' or 'the modernity' create a dangling modifier.

questions.passage:
A public library system tested a summer reading challenge at three branches. The program director claims that Cedar Branch had the strongest completion rate among participating children. The table shows the results.

Branch | Registered children | Completed goal
Cedar | 80 | 56
Maple | 120 | 72
Pine | 100 | 65
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: Pine Branch had the highest completion rate because 65 children completed the goal.
Cedar Branch had the highest completion rate, with 70% of its registered children finishing the goal.
Maple Branch had the highest completion rate because it had the most registered children.
All three branches had completion rates greater than 65%.
questions.explanation: Cedar's completion rate is 56 ÷ 80 = 70%; Maple's is 72 ÷ 120 = 60%; Pine's is 65 ÷ 100 = 65%. Therefore, Cedar had the highest rate even though Maple had the largest number of registered children.

questions.passage:
A museum consortium compared daily attendance on free-admission days and paid-admission days at three museums. The consortium's analyst notes that free admission did not raise attendance at every museum. The table shows average daily attendance.

Museum | Free day | Paid day
Harbor | 290 | 310
Riverside | 410 | 350
Northside | 520 | 470
questions.q: Which choice best describes the data in the table?
options: Paid-day attendance was higher than free-day attendance at every museum.
Free-day attendance was higher than paid-day attendance at Riverside and Northside, but lower at Harbor.
Northside had the largest difference between free-day and paid-day attendance.
Free-day attendance was higher than paid-day attendance at all three museums.
questions.explanation: Riverside's free-day average (410) exceeded its paid-day average (350), and Northside's (520) exceeded its paid-day average (470); Harbor's free-day average (290) was lower than its paid-day average (310). The largest difference was Riverside's 60 visitors per day, not Northside's 50.

questions.passage:
A team of ecologists hypothesized that increased shade lowers dissolved oxygen in small ponds. They measured average shade and average dissolved oxygen at three ponds on the same morning. The table shows their results.

Pond | Shade (%) | Dissolved oxygen (mg/L)
Alder | 10 | 8.4
Birch | 40 | 7.1
Cedar | 70 | 5.9
questions.q: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the team's hypothesis?
options: The three ponds had nearly identical dissolved oxygen levels despite different shade levels.
Birch Pond had the highest dissolved oxygen, which supports the hypothesis that shade lowers oxygen.
As shade increased from 10% at Alder to 70% at Cedar, average dissolved oxygen fell from 8.4 mg/L to 5.9 mg/L.
Alder Pond had the most shade and the lowest dissolved oxygen.
questions.explanation: The table shows oxygen decreasing as shade increases: 8.4 mg/L at 10% shade, 7.1 mg/L at 40% shade, and 5.9 mg/L at 70% shade. This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that greater shade is associated with lower dissolved oxygen.

questions.passage: Although the committee's final report was lengthy, its recommendations were ______: each proposed change was stated in a single sentence, without background discussion or extended justification.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: succinct
ornate
exhaustive
tentative
questions.explanation: The colon explains that each recommendation was stated in a single sentence without background discussion, so the recommendations were brief and to the point. Succinct means exactly that. Tentative would suggest uncertainty, ornate would suggest elaborate style, and exhaustive would suggest great completeness rather than brevity.

questions.passage: The director's staging of the play is notably ______: every gesture, pause, and lighting shift is calibrated to reinforce the production's central theme.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: haphazard
spontaneous
extravagant
deliberate
questions.explanation: The details are calibrated to support the theme, indicating careful and intentional planning, which deliberate conveys. Spontaneous and haphazard suggest lack of planning, while extravagant concerns lavishness rather than control.

questions.passage: Rather than offering a single explanation for the collapse, the historian presents a ______ account that weighs competing economic, environmental, and political factors without reducing the event to any one cause.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: nostalgic
multifaceted
terse
dogmatic
questions.explanation: The account considers several competing factors and refuses a single cause, so it is many-sided or multifaceted. Dogmatic would mean rigidly asserting one view, nostalgic would mean sentimental about the past, and terse would mean brief.

questions.passage: A team of educational psychologists hypothesized that a brief midday nap improves high school students' memory for vocabulary more effectively than a caffeinated drink does.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
options: Teachers reported that students often preferred afternoon classes to morning classes.
Students who took a 20-minute nap recalled more vocabulary words four hours later than students who had a caffeinated drink after the same study session.
Students who napped reported feeling more relaxed than students who drank caffeine.
Students who drank caffeine completed a vocabulary quiz faster than students who napped.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis concerns memory for vocabulary, so the most direct support would come from a comparison showing better later recall after napping than after caffeine. Feeling relaxed, quiz speed, and class-time preferences do not directly measure vocabulary memory.

questions.passage: Art historian Beatriz Molina hypothesized that the growing use of blue paint on houses in the port town of Marisol between 1850 and 1880 resulted from a new shipping route that made indigo dye cheaper, not from a shift in local taste.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Molina's hypothesis?
options: Shipping records show that indigo prices in Marisol fell sharply soon after the new route opened, and blue paint use rose first in neighborhoods closest to the port.
Blue paint remained equally common in inland towns that the new shipping route did not serve.
Fashion magazines from the period praised blue houses as more stylish than white ones.
Builders in Marisol used blue paint most often on the largest houses, which belonged to wealthy merchants.
questions.explanation: Molina's hypothesis ties blue paint to cheaper indigo made available by the new shipping route. A sharp price drop after the route opened, followed by the earliest rise in blue paint use near the port, directly supports that economic explanation. Magazine praise would support a taste explanation, while wealth or inland patterns do not show the route's effect.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Transit official Omar Haddad argues that replacing paper tickets and cash fares with a smartphone payment system will make bus riding more convenient and reduce fare evasion. He notes that riders could board faster and that the system would record every payment automatically. 

Text 2: Community advocate Renee Alvarez agrees that faster boarding would help, but she warns that a smartphone-only system would burden older riders and people without bank accounts. She argues that the transit agency should keep cash and card options available at all stations.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Alvarez most likely respond to Haddad's argument about convenience?
options: She would acknowledge the benefit of faster boarding while arguing that convenience must be balanced with access for riders who lack smartphones or bank accounts.
She would reject the idea that faster boarding could ever benefit a transit system.
She would claim that smartphone payment systems are too expensive for all riders, including those with bank accounts.
She would argue that fare evasion is the only issue that transit agencies should address.
questions.explanation: Alvarez agrees that faster boarding would help but warns that a smartphone-only system would exclude older riders and people without bank accounts. Her response would therefore treat convenience as valuable but insufficient without accessible alternatives. The text does not say she rejects faster boarding entirely or opposes it for all riders.

questions.passage:
Text 1: In an analysis of Rivertown's 1970s downtown pedestrian mall, historian Carla Nguyen argues that closing several blocks to cars created a lively public space where residents met, shopped, and attended outdoor events. She concludes that the mall strengthened the community's sense of connection.

Text 2: Urban planner Samuel Brooks notes that Rivertown's pedestrian mall initially attracted visitors but lost businesses as customers found parking inconvenient and as nearby suburban malls drew them away. He argues that the project's social benefits cannot be understood apart from its economic difficulties.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 1 highlights the mall's role in strengthening community, while Text 2 emphasizes the economic problems that caused businesses to leave.
Text 2 argues that the mall had no social benefits.
Text 1 and Text 2 both agree that the mall failed because parking was inconvenient.
Text 1 treats the mall as an economic failure, whereas Text 2 treats it as a social success.
questions.explanation: Nguyen focuses on the mall as a lively public space that strengthened community connection. Brooks shifts attention to the loss of businesses, inconvenient parking, and competition from suburban malls, showing the economic difficulties that shaped the project.

questions.passage: When a city tests a new express bus route, some riders worry that fewer stops will make service inconvenient for older residents and people with disabilities. A study of several transit systems found that express routes often attracted new riders while local bus ridership stayed steady. ______, concerns about access can lead neighborhood groups to oppose express routes even when the evidence is mixed.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: For instance,
Similarly,
Nevertheless,
As a result,
questions.explanation: The next sentence contrasts concerns about access with research findings that express routes can attract riders without reducing local ridership. “Nevertheless” marks that contrast. “As a result” and “Similarly” wrongly suggest that the concern follows from, or resembles, the study’s findings.

questions.passage: At a county fair, a beekeeper placed two identical hives in neighboring fields. Each day she played a recorded hum near one hive and left the other silent. After six weeks, the hives contained similar amounts of honey, though the hive exposed to the hum had built slightly more comb. The beekeeper concluded that the recorded hum probably ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: made the humming hive produce more honey than the silent hive
changed the number of bees in the hives
had little effect on the colonies’ honey production
caused the bees to stop building comb
questions.explanation: The two hives produced similar amounts of honey, so the hum probably had little effect on honey production. The slight increase in comb does not support a claim that the hum made the hive produce more honey, and no evidence concerns the number of bees.

questions.passage: In her history of a 1930s strike, historian Priya Desai begins not with the factory gates but with a community kitchen. She describes how strikers’ families organized meals, shared childcare, and raised funds. Desai argues that the strike’s success depended as much on these daily acts of cooperation as on the negotiations themselves. By focusing on the kitchen, she shows that labor movements are sustained by ordinary care as well as public protest.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Community kitchens were more important to the strike than negotiations were.
Desai’s history focuses mainly on the factory gates rather than on workers’ families.
The 1930s strike succeeded because workers avoided public protest.
A historian’s account of a strike emphasizes that daily cooperation helped sustain the labor movement.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that Desai’s history gives central attention to community kitchens and daily cooperation in order to reinterpret how a strike was sustained. It does not claim that kitchens mattered more than negotiations or that the strike avoided public protest.

questions.passage:
• The town’s old depot has been unused since it closed in 1998.
• A preservation group estimates that repairs would cost $1.2 million.
• The town council proposes turning the depot into a community art center with galleries and classrooms.
• More than 600 residents signed a petition supporting the art center.
questions.q: The student’s goal is to write a sentence for a grant application that presents the council’s proposal and the community support for it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The preservation group estimates that repairs would cost $1.2 million, which would provide galleries and classrooms.
Repairs to the town’s old depot, which has been unused since 1998, would cost an estimated $1.2 million.
The town council proposes turning the unused depot into a community art center, a plan supported by a petition signed by more than 600 residents.
More than 600 residents signed a petition, and the depot has been unused since 1998.
questions.explanation: The goal requires naming the council’s proposal and showing community support. The sentence about converting the depot into a community art center with a petition signed by more than 600 residents supplies both. Choices about repair costs or the unused building do not present the proposal and support together.

questions.passage: In the early 1900s, many cities built public bathhouses to improve hygiene in crowded neighborhoods. The bathhouses offered warm water and laundry facilities at low cost, and they were popular with recent immigrants. ______, many cities closed them within a few decades, as private indoor plumbing became more common and maintenance costs rose.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: For example,
Likewise,
However,
Therefore,
questions.explanation: The first sentences describe benefits and popularity, while the final clause explains that cities closed the bathhouses. “However” signals this contrast. “Therefore” would incorrectly suggest that popularity and low cost caused the closures.

questions.passage: A team of psychologists asked volunteers to memorize a list of words while hearing either quiet room noise or recorded music with lyrics. On an immediate test, the music group recalled slightly fewer words than the quiet group. When both groups returned a week later and were tested in silence, however, the groups performed almost identically. The results suggest that the music’s effect on memory was ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: stronger after a week than at first
temporary rather than lasting
caused by the room noise rather than the music
the same in both testing sessions
questions.explanation: The music group performed slightly worse only on the immediate test; a week later, the groups performed almost identically. That pattern supports a temporary effect, not a lasting or stronger one. The immediate difference also rules out saying performance was the same in both sessions.

questions.passage: In a magazine article about the history of the shopping cart, writer Daniel Cho begins with a 1937 patent drawing of a folding cart. He notes that shoppers initially resisted the new design, preferring baskets they could carry. Cho then explains how stores changed their layouts to make carts more convenient, and he concludes that the cart succeeded not because of the invention alone but because stores redesigned the shopping experience around it.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: to list the reasons a patent was denied in 1937
to describe the exact dimensions of a 1937 folding cart
to argue that shoppers today should use baskets instead of carts
to explain how an article argues that a familiar invention succeeded through changes in store design
questions.explanation: The text summarizes how Daniel Cho explains the shopping cart’s success through changes in store layouts and the shopping experience, not through the invention alone. It does not provide dimensions, recommend baskets, or discuss a patent denial.

questions.passage:
• The city opened a weekend farmers market in the old train station lot in June.
• Vendors sold $48,000 in goods during the market’s first month.
• A survey found that 71% of nearby residents said they shopped at the market.
• Some nearby businesses reported fewer parking spaces available on Saturdays.
• The market operates Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m.
questions.q: The student’s goal is to write a sentence for a city council report that summarizes both an economic benefit and a drawback of the market. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Some nearby businesses reported fewer parking spaces on Saturdays, a problem that reduced the market’s vendor sales.
Vendors sold $48,000 in goods during the market’s first month, and 71% of nearby residents said they shopped there.
The market operates Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., and some nearby businesses reported fewer parking spaces available on Saturdays.
During its first month, the weekend farmers market generated $48,000 in vendor sales, though some nearby businesses reported fewer parking spaces available on Saturdays.
questions.explanation: Vendor sales of $48,000 provide an economic benefit, and reduced parking on Saturdays is a drawback. The other choices either leave out the drawback, leave out the economic benefit, or wrongly claim that parking problems reduced sales.

questions.passage: The Riverbend Community Center extended its Saturday hours from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. last fall. ______, attendance at its evening art classes nearly doubled during the fall session.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: As a result,
Nevertheless,
In comparison,
For example,
questions.explanation: Extending Saturday hours plausibly caused the increase in evening art class attendance, so “As a result” expresses the causal link. “Nevertheless” and “In comparison” signal contrast, and “For example” would mislabel the increase as an illustration rather than an outcome.

questions.passage:
• Westside High School’s robotics team built a small machine that sorts recycling by material.
• The team tested it at the school cafeteria for two weeks.
• It correctly sorted 92% of cans and bottles.
• It occasionally jammed when labels were wet.
• Team members plan to add a drying fan before the district competition.
questions.q: The student’s goal is to write a sentence for a school newsletter that explains the machine’s performance and an improvement the team plans to make. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The robotics team built a small machine that sorts recycling by material for the district competition.
The robotics team’s recycling sorter correctly sorted 92% of cans and bottles during a two-week cafeteria test, and the team plans to add a drying fan to reduce jams from wet labels.
The team plans to add a drying fan before the district competition because wet labels often jam other machines.
During a two-week cafeteria test, the recycling sorter correctly sorted 92% of cans and bottles, which impressed cafeteria staff.
questions.explanation: The sentence must include the sorter’s measured performance and the planned improvement. The 92% sorting rate and the drying fan to reduce wet-label jams meet both requirements. Choices that mention only the machine, only the plan, or an inaccurate problem with other machines do not.

questions.passage: The botanist Dr. Amara Okafor______ had studied desert grasses for more than a decade, warned that the restoration plan would need careful irrigation. Her advice persuaded the county to delay planting until the fall.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: , who
: who
who
; who
questions.explanation: The clause beginning “who had studied desert grasses…” is nonrestrictive, so it must be set off by a comma before “who” and by the comma already present after “decade.” A semicolon or colon cannot introduce this clause, and omitting the comma creates incorrect punctuation around the nonrestrictive clause.

questions.passage: The curator wanted visitors to see how the region's artists had responded to environmental change over time. To make that story easy to follow, she organized the exhibit around three themes______, adaptation, and memory.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: , migration
migration
; migration
: migration
questions.explanation: A colon appropriately introduces the list that specifies the three themes. A comma or semicolon does not correctly introduce this list, and omitting punctuation leaves the list improperly attached to “three themes.”

questions.passage: The first attempt to restore the wetland was inexpensive but slow______ it gave volunteers time to document which native plants returned first. That record helped the group plan the next phase of planting.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: : however,
, however,
however,
; however,
questions.explanation: The sentence joins two independent clauses, and the conjunctive adverb “however” follows the first clause. Standard English requires a semicolon before “however” in this structure; a comma would create a comma splice, and omitting punctuation or using a colon before “however” is not correct here.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The collection of oral histories, which students began recording in 2019, ______ researchers with access to details absent from official records.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: have provided
provide
were providing
provides
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “collection,” not the plural noun “histories” inside the prepositional phrase. The singular present-tense verb “provides” agrees with that subject.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: Neither the principal nor the teachers at Riverside High School ______ satisfied with the original plan for the new gymnasium, so the committee scheduled another meeting.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: were
was
is
has been
questions.explanation: With a “neither…nor” construction, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject is the plural noun “teachers,” so the plural verb “were” is required.

questions.topic: Form, structure and sense (grammar and usage)
questions.passage: The research team spent several weeks analyzing survey responses from more than eight hundred residents about changes in their neighborhoods. After analyzing the survey data for several weeks, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: identifying the pattern was what the researchers did after the responses.
a pattern was identified by the researchers that had been hidden in the responses.
the pattern hidden in the responses was identified by the researchers.
the researchers identified a pattern that had been hidden in the responses.
questions.explanation: The introductory participial phrase “After analyzing the survey data…” must describe the subject of the main clause. Only the choice beginning “the researchers identified…” gives the correct subject, the researchers, for that phrase.

questions.passage: When the town of Willow Creek opened its first public library in 1911, the building had two rooms and fewer than five hundred books. Over the next century, the library moved three times, added a children's wing, and began lending tools and seeds as well as books. Today, residents use the library not only to borrow materials but also to attend language classes and community meetings. The library's role, in other words, has expanded far beyond what its founders imagined.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The Willow Creek library was founded with an unusually large collection.
The library has moved three times because residents wanted a larger children's wing.
Tool and seed lending are the library's most popular services.
A small-town library has grown into a broader community resource over time.
questions.explanation: The text traces the library from a small collection in two rooms to a place offering classes, meetings, and new kinds of lending. The other choices either contradict the text or add unsupported claims about popularity or causes.

questions.passage: Many birds use magnetic cues to navigate, but how they sense magnetic fields remains debated. A team of biologists tested whether European robins rely on a protein in their eyes called cryptochrome 4. In the experiment, robins with normal cryptochrome 4 oriented toward their migratory direction under dim blue light, while robins whose cryptochrome 4 had been reduced appeared disoriented under the same light. The researchers caution that the results do not prove that the protein is the only sensor involved, but they do suggest that it plays a role in the birds' magnetic sense.
questions.q: According to the text, which choice best describes the result for robins whose cryptochrome 4 had been reduced?
options: They navigated using stars instead of magnetic cues.
They produced more cryptochrome 4 than other robins did.
They appeared disoriented under dim blue light.
They migrated in the opposite direction under normal light.
questions.explanation: The text states that robins whose cryptochrome 4 had been reduced appeared disoriented under the same dim blue light. The other choices introduce behaviors or effects that the passage does not describe.

questions.passage:
A transportation team surveyed 300 residents in three neighborhoods—100 in each—about their primary way of commuting to work. The table shows the percentage of respondents in each neighborhood who reported each mode.

Neighborhood | Drove alone | Public transit | Walked/biked
North | 62% | 21% | 17%
Central | 38% | 40% | 22%
South | 55% | 18% | 27%
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim that Central residents were more likely than residents of the other neighborhoods to use public transit?
options: In Central, 40% of respondents reported using public transit, compared with 21% in North and 18% in South.
In South, 27% of respondents walked or biked, compared with 22% in Central and 17% in North.
In Central, 38% of respondents reported driving alone, compared with 55% in South and 62% in North.
In Central, 40% of respondents reported using public transit, while 38% drove alone and 22% walked or biked.
questions.explanation: The claim is about public transit in Central compared with the other neighborhoods, and the correct choice directly compares Central's 40% public-transit share with the lower shares in North and South. The other choices either discuss a different mode of travel or provide Central's figures without the comparison needed to support the claim.

questions.passage:
A team of ecologists studied three restored meadows to examine whether native plant cover is associated with bee species richness. They surveyed each meadow in 2018 and again in 2023.

Meadow | Native plant cover 2018 | Native plant cover 2023 | Bee species 2018 | Bee species 2023
A | 20% | 35% | 12 | 17
B | 45% | 50% | 18 | 20
C | 60% | 55% | 22 | 19
questions.q: Which choice best describes a conclusion about the relationship between native plant cover and bee species richness that is supported by the table?
options: Bee species richness was higher in 2018 than in 2023 at all three meadows.
The meadow with the lowest native plant cover in 2023 had the greatest number of bee species in 2023.
In each meadow, the change in native plant cover from 2018 to 2023 was accompanied by a change in the same direction in the number of bee species observed.
Native plant cover decreased in every meadow between 2018 and 2023, and bee species richness decreased as well.
questions.explanation: In every meadow, native plant cover and bee species counts moved in the same direction from 2018 to 2023: both rose in two meadows and both fell in one meadow. The other choices make claims that are contradicted by the table.

questions.passage: During the first weeks of the community theater's production, the director worried that the cast's timing was loose and the scenes felt uneven. By opening night, however, the actors moved through the final act with such ______ that even the stage crew stopped checking the script backstage.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: precision
hesitation
confusion
delay
questions.explanation: The contrast with the early weeks' loose timing and uneven scenes shows that the actors became smooth and exact by opening night, so 'precision' fits. 'Hesitation,' 'confusion,' and 'delay' would imply continued uncertainty, not the improvement described.

questions.passage: The city's new riverfront trail was designed to give residents a safe place to walk and bike. ______, the trail includes benches, drinking fountains, and shade structures that make longer outings more comfortable.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: In addition
In contrast
Nevertheless
As a result
questions.explanation: The second sentence adds details about features of the trail that support its use, so an additive transition such as 'In addition' is appropriate. 'Nevertheless' and 'In contrast' signal contrast, while 'As a result' incorrectly presents the features as an effect.

questions.passage: A team of biologists studied whether a night-blooming flower attracts moths mainly by scent rather than by color. The team grew two groups of plants with identical flower colors: one group had normal fragrant flowers, while the other had flowers whose scent had been chemically removed. At night, moths visited the fragrant flowers more than twice as often as they visited the unscented flowers. ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Moths visited the unscented flowers only when the fragrant flowers were unavailable.
The moths' preference shows that they are unable to perceive flower color at night.
This result supports the idea that scent played a stronger role than color in attracting the moths.
The result proves that removing scent changes the color of night-blooming flowers.
questions.explanation: Because the two groups had identical flower colors, the greater visitation to fragrant flowers points to scent as the stronger attraction. The result does not show that moths cannot perceive color, change flower color, or that visits occurred only under a specific condition.

questions.passage: Text 1: In a policy brief, librarian Maya Chen argues that digitizing local historical records helps small historical societies share their collections with students and researchers who cannot visit in person. Even modest grants, she writes, can turn a few boxes of letters into a widely used online archive. Text 2: Archivist Daniel Ortiz agrees that digitization broadens access, but he cautions that organizations often scan only materials that seem visually interesting or likely to attract website visitors. Less striking records—routine ledgers, meeting minutes, ordinary correspondence—may be left out, giving online users a distorted view of the past.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Ortiz most likely respond to Chen's argument?
options: He would claim that small historical societies cannot benefit from modest grants.
He would support expanding digital access but warn that choices about which materials to digitize can make online collections unrepresentative.
He would argue that digitization should be abandoned because physical archives are always more accurate.
He would insist that visually interesting records are the most historically valuable materials.
questions.explanation: Ortiz agrees with Chen that digitization broadens access, but he adds a concern about selective scanning and distorted online collections. He does not reject digitization or deny the value of grants; his warning is about the representativeness of what gets digitized.

questions.passage: Although the biographer admired her subject's achievements, she refused to write a ______ account; her book gives full attention to his failed projects, his stubbornness, and the colleagues he alienated.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: technical
exhaustive
idealized
hostile
questions.explanation: The clause after the semicolon shows that the biographer includes failures and difficult traits, so she avoids an overly flattering or idealized account. 'Hostile' goes too far because admiration is also mentioned, while 'exhaustive' and 'technical' do not capture the contrast with praising only achievements.

questions.passage: To test whether urban foxes adjust their activity to avoid people, a team of ecologists placed motion-sensitive cameras in parks across a city. Some cameras were near busy playgrounds, and others were in quiet wooded areas. The cameras recorded more fox sightings at night than during the day at both kinds of sites. The team also found that foxes were seen at busy sites mostly between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m., when foot traffic was lowest. ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: These findings prove that artificial light, rather than human activity, controls fox behavior.
These findings indicate that foxes are equally active at busy and quiet sites at all hours.
These findings show that foxes avoid all parks with playgrounds during every part of the night.
These findings suggest that although foxes were generally nocturnal, their timing at busy sites was associated with periods of low human presence.
questions.explanation: The data show a nocturnal pattern at both site types and activity at busy sites concentrated when people were least present, supporting a more nuanced conclusion about timing. The evidence does not show complete avoidance, equal activity at all hours, or prove that artificial light is the controlling factor.

questions.passage: Some urban planners predicted that closing a downtown street to cars would hurt nearby shops by reducing customers. ______, a yearlong count found that sales at shops on the closed block rose slightly, and most owners supported making the closure permanent.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: For instance
Similarly
However
Therefore
questions.explanation: The second sentence presents a result that contradicts the planners' prediction, so 'However' is appropriate. 'Therefore' and 'Similarly' signal cause or similarity, and 'For instance' would introduce an example rather than a contrast.

questions.passage: Text 1: Historian Elena Park argues that streetcar suburbs in the early twentieth century were shaped primarily by transportation technology: rail lines allowed middle-class families to live farther from downtown. Text 2: Historian Marcus Green responds that in Riverton, developers often built streetcar lines only after zoning and lending policies had already encouraged single-family homes along the route. He concludes that public policy, rather than the streetcar alone, determined where growth occurred.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 2 focuses on a city where rail lines were never built or used.
Text 2 argues that streetcars had no influence on suburban growth anywhere.
Text 2 qualifies Text 1's emphasis on transportation technology by offering a case in which policy also shaped suburban development.
Text 2 restates Text 1's argument using a different example.
questions.explanation: Green does not deny that streetcars mattered; he challenges Park's emphasis on technology as the primary cause by pointing to policy in Riverton. The other choices misstate his position by making him wholly dismiss streetcars or merely repeat Park's claim.

questions.passage: The novelist's style is often described as ______: her sentences are so spare that a single discarded detail can feel like a major revelation.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: ornate
tentative
economical
digressive
questions.explanation: The colon explains that the sentences are 'so spare,' meaning the style withholds or uses very few words, so 'economical' is the best fit. 'Ornate' means elaborate, and 'digressive' means wandering off topic, both opposite to spare; 'tentative' suggests uncertainty rather than restraint.

questions.passage: A team of public health researchers found that residents of a neighborhood with newly installed sidewalk lighting reported feeling safer walking after dark than residents of a similar neighborhood without the lighting did. The researchers concluded that the lighting itself caused the increase in reported safety. ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Therefore, sidewalk lighting is popular in many cities around the country.
In addition, some residents said they preferred brighter sidewalks.
However, the neighborhood with new lighting had also recently begun a well-publicized community police foot patrol.
For example, the neighborhood without lighting had several older streetlamps.
questions.explanation: The conclusion attributes the safety reports to lighting, but a simultaneous police foot patrol would provide another explanation, weakening the causal claim. The preference comment and popularity statement do not address whether lighting caused the change, and older streetlamps elsewhere do not explain the difference.

questions.passage: At the Riverside Community Garden, coordinator Priya Patel noticed that plots near the tool shed produced fewer tomatoes than plots on the garden’s eastern edge. Both areas received the same amount of water and sunlight, but the soil near the shed had been repeatedly compacted by foot traffic. After volunteers loosened the soil in several shed-side plots and added compost, tomato yields in those plots rose sharply. These results most strongly suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: foot traffic near a tool shed harms tomato plants mainly by reducing their exposure to sunlight
adding compost alone can increase tomato yields regardless of soil compaction
tomato plants on an eastern edge will always outperform those planted near a tool shed
compacted soil can limit tomato production even when water and sunlight are adequate
questions.explanation: The loosened, composted plots produced more tomatoes after the compaction was addressed, while water and sunlight were already equal. This supports the idea that compacted soil limited growth rather than inadequate sunlight or poor garden location; the option about compost alone overstates the evidence because the volunteers also loosened the soil.

questions.passage: At a county historical society, curator Luis Ortega found that a 1915 catalog for a local department store listed sewing machines on credit but did not list ready-made dresses. By 1925, the same store devoted three catalog pages to inexpensive ready-made dresses and reduced its sewing machine display to a single model. Ortega argues that this shift alone does not prove that local households stopped sewing, since many families could have continued mending clothes at home while buying new dresses for work. His argument suggests that the catalog change ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: was caused mainly by a decline in the quality of sewing machines
proves that local families had abandoned sewing machines by 1925
shows that ready-made dresses had become more expensive than sewing machines
may reflect changing shopping habits without showing that home sewing disappeared
questions.explanation: Ortega says the shift in the catalog does not prove that households stopped sewing and notes that families might have kept mending while buying ready-made dresses. Thus the catalog change may show new shopping patterns without proving that home sewing disappeared.

questions.passage: During a drought, a city's reservoirs fell below 30% of capacity. The city began offering rebates for replacing lawns with native plants. After one year, water use per household had fallen by 12%, but the city’s total water use had fallen by only 3%. The city population had grown during that year, and many commercial properties were not eligible for the rebates. These facts suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: commercial properties used less water than households before the rebate program began
the rebate program reduced household water use, though other factors limited the decline in total water use
native plants eliminated the need for irrigation in participating households
population growth had no effect on the city’s total water use
questions.explanation: Household water use fell by 12%, but total city use fell only 3% while the population grew and many commercial properties were excluded from rebates. That pattern supports a decline among participating households, with other factors keeping the total decline smaller.

questions.passage: The city council expected residents to oppose replacing a downtown parking lot with a small park because the plan removed forty parking spaces. After the park opened, a survey found that 61% of respondents supported keeping it. Support was highest among people who lived within a half mile, but even a majority of nearby shop owners said deliveries had not become noticeably harder. The council’s initial expectation, in other words, did not match the concerns residents actually voiced.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It contrasts a prediction with survey results that complicate that prediction.
It describes a policy and then lists arguments for reversing it.
It presents a widely accepted claim and then offers an example that illustrates the claim.
It compares two groups’ opinions without stating a conclusion.
questions.explanation: The text sets up the council's expectation of opposition, then presents survey results showing support and limited delivery problems. It concludes by noting that this expectation did not match residents' concerns, so the structure contrasts a prediction with complicating results.

questions.passage:
• Program: Saturday morning Fix-It Clinic at the Northside Community Center.
• In its first month, volunteers repaired 65 small appliances.
• The clinic has saved residents an estimated $4,800 in replacement costs.
• In a follow-up survey, 80% of participants said they would return with another item.
• The center will hold the clinic twice monthly next spring.
questions.q: The student’s goal is to write a sentence for a grant application that emphasizes both the clinic’s financial benefit and its popularity. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The Fix-It Clinic, which the center will hold twice monthly next spring, repaired 65 small appliances in its first month.
Volunteers at the Fix-It Clinic repaired 65 small appliances in its first month, and the center will hold the clinic twice monthly next spring.
The Fix-It Clinic saved residents an estimated $4,800 in replacement costs and will operate twice monthly next spring.
In its first month, the Fix-It Clinic repaired 65 small appliances, saving residents an estimated $4,800, and 80% of participants said they would return with another item.
questions.explanation: The grant sentence must combine a financial benefit with evidence of popularity. The repaired appliances and $4,800 saved show the financial benefit, while the 80% who would return shows popularity; the other choices leave out one of the two required emphases or focus on the future schedule.
